blocks.text: Atomic spectra are seen when atoms emit or absorb light of particular wavelengths: these are emission and absorption spectra. They are evidence that electrons in atoms can move only between fixed (discrete) energy levels. When electrons absorb energy they move from lower to higher energy levels; the excited electrons then give out energy as they return to lower levels, forming an emission spectrum.

items: An emission spectrum is produced by heating a low-pressure gas. When an electron drops to a lower level it emits a photon whose wavelength matches the energy difference, so the spectrum is a set of distinct coloured lines on a black background.

blocks.alt: Top: a black strip with four coloured lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm, axis Wavelength, lambda (nm). Below: energy levels n = 2, 3, 4 and 5 with three thick downward arrows ending at n = 2, from n = 3 (pink), n = 4 (light blue) and n = 5 (dark blue); a wavy photon of the same colour leaves each to the left.
blocks.caption: Figure 29.2: Hydrogen emission spectrum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 29.2).

items: An absorption spectrum is produced by passing white light through a cool, low-pressure gas. Only photons with exactly the energy needed to excite electrons are absorbed, so the spectrum is a continuous band crossed by dark lines. The dark lines are at the same wavelengths as the bright lines of the emission spectrum of the same element: an absorption spectrum is like a photographic negative of the emission spectrum.

blocks.alt: Top: a continuous colour band from violet to red crossed by dark lines at 410, 434, 486 and 656 nm, axis Wavelength, lambda (nm). Below: energy levels n = 2, 3, 4 and 5 with three thick upward arrows from n = 2 to n = 3 (pink), n = 4 (light blue) and n = 5 (dark blue); a wavy photon of the same colour comes in from the left to each arrow.
blocks.caption: Figure 29.3: Hydrogen absorption spectrum (original drawing after the textbook's Figure 29.3).
